teaser: Two AI sessions sharing nothing passed keys, a certificate, images and an encrypted message through QR codes and a screenshot.
core_idea: A person relaying screenshots between two isolated AI sessions is a lossless channel for QR codes up to the format's 2,953-byte limit, enough for keys, certificates, compressed images and encrypted, signed messages; the trust still comes from signatures and a human checking fingerprints, and QR codes are a friendlier way to move keys than blobs of text.

nodes.label: The failures
nodes.summary: No reading by eye; a lost key.

nodes.label: Friendlier than text blobs
nodes.summary: Keys a person can see and hand over.

quotes.text: one of those super interesting sort of serendipity things that happens when you're doing a bunch of experiments
QR codes are way more user friendly than what we were using to share the vault keys and the encrypted messages.
A signature proves the bytes did not change; a key that travels inside its own message proves nothing about who sent it.

figures.caption: Text, then JSON, then binary, then PKI, each in one QR code: a plain message, a signed JSON key offer, a compressed vector graphic, a photo-like image, an X.509 certificate and an encrypted message, passed between two Claude sessions by screenshot and paste, and each decoded and verified on arrival. Made by Session B.

The screenshot that carried four QR codes from one session to the other, as Session A showed them in its chat: from a short message to the largest code the format allows, the one on the right, 2,953 bytes.

Left: the bytes in each code of the graded test set, from 53 for a short message to 2,953 for the largest code, with its QR version. Right: a version 40 code holds 2,953 bytes written raw, 2,864 as base45 and 2,214 as base64.
Two images inside single QR codes, each next to the image rebuilt from its decoded bytes: the whole infographic as compressed SVG, 539 bytes, and a 480 by 320 photo-like image as AVIF, 2,083 bytes.

The key exchange by screenshot: Session B publishes an X25519 public key as a QR code; the person carries it; Session A encrypts and signs a message to it and returns it as a QR code of 1,329 bytes; Session B decrypts it.
Session B's reply to the first QR code: it decoded the signed key offer, verified the Ed25519 signature, and pointed out that this proves integrity, not authenticity.
